title: Why Japan Never Actually Abolished the Hanko Stamp
hook: Japan scrapped the hanko for 15,000 government forms in 2021, then made its most important stamp harder to replace than ever.
target_query: did japan get rid of the hanko stamp
free_section_html:
No, Japan did not get rid of the hanko (also called inkan, a carved personal seal used instead of a signature). What happened between 2020 and 2021 was narrower: the government reviewed roughly 15,000 administrative procedures that required a physical stamp and removed the requirement from all but a small fraction of them. Tax filings, many labor contracts, and routine city-office paperwork no longer need ink. But one category of hanko was left almost entirely untouched, and it is the one that matters most: the jitsuin, or registered seal.

A jitsuin is a hanko that a resident has formally registered with their local ward or city office, a process called inkan toroku. Once registered, that person can request an inkan shomeisho, a government-issued certificate proving that a specific stamp impression belongs to them. This pairing of seal and certificate is what actually carries legal weight in Japan, not the stamp itself. Anyone can carve a look-alike hanko in a train station kiosk in ten minutes; only a registered seal backed by a certificate can transfer land, execute a will, or set up a company.

Real estate transfers, inheritance division agreements, auto purchase loans, and corporate registration still run on this system almost unchanged since the postwar Civil Code. The 2021 reform explicitly excluded these because they are written into statutes like the Real Property Registration Act and the Commercial Registration Act, not just bureaucratic custom. Changing them means amending law, not just agency policy, which is a slower and more contested process.

So the digital-government campaign eliminated the hanko where it was mostly ceremonial, in daily office life, while leaving it fully intact where it functions as identity infrastructure. That split raises a harder question: why has a country that builds bullet trains and industrial robots been unable, or unwilling, to replace a seal-and-paper verification system for something as high-stakes as who owns a house.
paid_body_html:
The seal that survived the purge

When Japan's digital reform push gathered pace under the Suga administration in 2020, the target was explicit: a bureaucracy where citizens routinely carried a personal stamp to city hall for procedures that, in most countries, require nothing more than a signature or a login. The Administrative Procedures Bureau's review found that the vast majority of the roughly 15,000 hanko-requiring procedures could be handled with a signature, an online form, or nothing at all. Within about a year, hanko requirements were dropped from the great majority of them.

The exceptions were concentrated in a narrow but consequential band of law: real property registration, commercial and corporate registration, notarized wills, and certain family court filings. These are governed by statutes that predate the digital reform entirely, some tracing to the postwar Civil Code and the Real Property Registration Act. A ward office can stop asking for a stamp on a childcare subsidy form by internal circular. It cannot change what a court or the Legal Affairs Bureau accepts as proof of intent to sell a house without amending the underlying law.

How the registered seal actually works

The mechanism is worth understanding because it explains why the system is so sticky. A resident registers a specific hanko design with their municipal office, which keeps the impression on file. From that point, the resident can request an inkan shomeisho, a certificate that states, in effect: this impression, made by this seal, belongs to this named person as of this date. The certificate, not the seal, is the actual legal proof; the stamp is simply the physical key that reproduces a registered pattern.

This is why a jitsuin used for buying an apartment or dividing an inherited estate is treated with a level of seriousness that a casual hanko, bought for a few dollars and used to acknowledge receiving a parcel, never carries. Losing a registered seal, or having one stolen along with the registration card, is closer in practical risk to losing a passport than to losing a rubber stamp. Ward offices in Tokyo and elsewhere handle a steady stream of cases each year involving fraudulent use of registered seals in property and inheritance disputes, which is one reason courts and legal scholars have been cautious about loosening the requirement rather than eager to.

A parallel system, not a replacement

Japan does have a functioning digital identity credential, the My Number card, tied to a national personal identification number system introduced in 2015 and expanded significantly since 2021. It supports electronic tax filing through the e-Tax system and, increasingly, medical insurance verification. But the My Number card and the jitsuin were built to solve different problems and have not been merged. My Number authenticates a person to a government computer system. The jitsuin, backed by its certificate, authenticates a person's intent on a specific paper document that a notary, a bank, or a court can physically examine years later.

Efforts to bridge the two exist. Since 2023, some real estate and corporate registration procedures have allowed electronic signatures verified through My Number as an alternative path, and the Ministry of Justice has run pilot programs for fully electronic company incorporation. Adoption has been slow, partly because banks, notaries, and older business owners are more comfortable with a system they and their institutions have used for decades, and partly because the electronic alternative requires hardware, an IC card reader or compatible smartphone, that not every small business or elderly landowner has on hand.

Why the craft persists

The commercial hanko trade has shrunk from its postwar peak, and neighborhoods once dense with seal-carving shops, such as parts of Kuramae in Tokyo, have seen many workshops close or shift toward decorative or ceremonial seals rather than everyday stamps. But shops that specialize in registered seals, often carved from buffalo horn, boxwood, or titanium and priced from several thousand to tens of thousands of yen, have not seen comparable decline. A registered seal is typically a one-time purchase meant to last a lifetime and, in some families, get passed down, which insulates that segment of the trade from the same volume drop affecting cheap, disposable stamps.

What actually changes next

The realistic trajectory is not abolition but slow substitution at the margins. Legal scholars and Justice Ministry officials involved in registration reform have generally described the goal as offering electronic alternatives alongside the seal system rather than forcing a switch, given how much of Japan's property and inheritance law is written around the assumption that a physical, verifiable mark of intent exists on paper. Full replacement would require rewriting core provisions of the Civil Code and the registration statutes, a process that moves in years, not budget cycles.

In practice, this means a Japanese resident today can go months without touching a hanko for ordinary bureaucratic life, then find themselves at a notary's office, seal and registration certificate in hand, the day they inherit their parents' house. The 2021 reform did not end the hanko era. It clarified which parts of that era were bureaucratic habit and which were load-bearing legal infrastructure, and left the second category standing.
key_takeaways: Japan's 2020-2021 reform removed hanko requirements from most of roughly 15,000 administrative procedures but excluded real estate, inheritance, and corporate registration.
The registered seal, or jitsuin, gets its legal force from a certificate (inkan shomeisho) issued by a municipal office, not from the physical stamp alone.
These exceptions exist because they are written into statutes like the Real Property Registration Act, which require legislative change rather than agency policy to alter.
Japan's My Number digital ID system runs alongside the hanko system rather than replacing it, with electronic alternatives available for some but not most property and corporate filings since 2023.
Hanko carving shops that specialize in registered seals have been more resilient than those selling everyday casual stamps.
meta_title: Did Japan Get Rid of the Hanko Stamp? Not Entirely
meta_description: Japan dropped hanko rules for 15,000 procedures, but the registered seal used for real estate and inheritance is more entrenched than ever. Here's why.
